more.summary: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope has revealed an ancient galaxy cluster with an unexpectedly dense concentration of dark matter, challenging theories about how the universe developed. The discovery also uncovered a surprising connection between scattered starlight and invisible dark matter that could transform how astronomers study the early cosmos.

more.title: Drier Texas rivers support simpler food webs and higher animal productivity, study finds
more.summary: Global warming is often treated as synonymous with climate change, but rising temperatures are only one consequence of the human-driven phenomenon. Changes in rainfall patterns are another, but their effects on ecosystems are less understood.

more.title: Faster molecular simulations identify promising diamond defects for quantum computers and sensors
more.summary: A faster way of finding the best diamond-based materials for quantum computers has been developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL). The new approach has already identified promising materials for practical quantum sensors and computers that could one day transform scientific research as a whole.

more.title: New method helps researchers study proteins involved in plant health, disease
more.summary: Plants—like people—come in all shapes and sizes. And just like scientists want to understand the components of the human body to treat disease and improve our lives, they also want to understand how plants thrive, develop disease, succumb or survive.

more.title: Humans and songbirds hear the same sounds, but organize them differently
more.summary: Researchers from the University of Amsterdam and Leiden University have discovered that humans and songbirds use markedly different strategies to recognize sequences of complex sounds. The findings shed new light on how biology and experience shape the way we perceive complex sounds, with implications for music and speech.

more.title: Researchers uncover multiple genetic paths that lead to mottled feathers in chickens
more.summary: The white-tipped feathers found in many chicken breeds may look like variations of the same decorative pattern, but new research shows that they do not all share the same genetic origin.

more.title: Want more women CEOs? Start with company structure, research finds
more.summary: Women managers are significantly more likely to be promoted to CEO at companies organized into separate business units—each with its own revenues, costs and bottom line—than at companies that operate as a single, stand-alone entity, a new study led by the University of Massachusetts Amherst finds.

more.title: Licube wants to be the fuel provider to the fusion power industry — see how at TechCrunch Disrupt
more.author: Tim De Chant
more.summary: Fusion power plants will need a lot of lithium, and Licube is preparing to be a key supplier.

more.title: 3D map of rice development charts gene activity across plant's entire life cycle
more.summary: Rice is one of the world's most familiar staple foods, but how does a single cell develop into a rice plant with specialized tissues and organs? A new study offers a detailed look at this process through a three-dimensional (3D) spatiotemporal atlas covering 10 organs and 61 developmental stages across the rice life cycle, from seed to seed.

more.title: Giraffe Bio aims its bespoke biomolecules at the looming copper shortage
more.author: Tim De Chant
more.summary: As AI data centers and EVs drive up demand for copper, Giraffe Bio has unearthed a $6.4 million seed round to help miners extract more of the mineral.

more.title: Niobia takes the guesswork out of some of tech’s most expensive mistakes
more.author: Zack Whittaker
more.summary: The San Francisco startup aims to help battery and chip manufacturers identify defects on production lines, reducing downtime and costly mistakes.

more.title: They war-gamed dimming the Sun. It went even worse than you think.
more.author: Karl Mathiesen, WIRED.com
more.summary: Solar geoengineering simulation shows what happens when geopolitics takes over.

more.title: Black women in food industries face systemic roadblocks
more.summary: Lilly Jan was perplexed and a little annoyed. Last year, Jan, an assistant teaching professor in the Cornell Nolan School of Hotel Administration in the Cornell SC Johnson College of Business, was trying to collect information on food industry businesses owned by Black women.

more.title: Simple cleaning steps could curb deadly fungal disease risks for Australia's wild reptiles
more.summary: With spring underway and the weather warming, reptiles are on the move in suburbs, parks and scrubland across Australia. Snake catchers and wildlife caregivers are responding to calls for help, and reptile enthusiasts—known as "herpers"—are heading outdoors in search of their next sighting.

more.title: The 2026 Startup Battlefield Top 20: From organs to orbit and everything in between
more.author: Isabelle Johannessen
more.summary: Twenty founders just earned their shot at Disrupt glory. They're headed to the main stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to compete for the $100,000 prize and the coveted Disrupt Cup.

more.title: Ultrashort laser pulses offer a new way to probe electrons' quantum geometry
more.summary: Researchers at Friedrich Schiller University Jena and the University of Regensburg have developed a method for determining, using light, a quantum property of electrons that has hitherto been difficult to access. The focus is on what is known as Berry curvature—a quantity that describes certain geometric properties of the quantum mechanical states of electrons.

more.title: Solar industry spends to flip control of Georgia utility commission
more.author: Julian Spector
more.summary: Voters will have a chance to pick their utility regulators in nine states this November. But Georgia is one of the only states that could flip party control of its public utility commission, an often overlooked institution that determines how much people’s energy bills will rise. Last year, as energy affordability…

more.title: Patterned X-rays map 3D chemical structures faster with fewer measurements
more.summary: Seeing inside an object is one thing; seeing exactly what it is made of, in three dimensions, is far more difficult. Now, researchers at Bar-Ilan University and collaborating institutions have developed a new X-ray imaging technique that can map the three-dimensional chemical composition of an object 43 times faster than conventional approaches, while using more than 97% less measurement data.

more.title: Optical skyrmions can control the motion of magnetic skyrmions
more.summary: Magnetic skyrmions (MSks) are swirling patterns of magnetization that form inside certain magnetic materials. They can behave like actual particles in many ways, exhibiting a stable internal structure and distinct boundaries. Because they are extremely small and can be pushed around with relatively little energy, MSks are regarded as promising information carriers in emerging technologies, including low-power…
